## What are we trying to understand?

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson cp-lesson"><p>A college researcher wants to understand whether attending a study-skills workshop is associated with meeting a criterion on a hypothetical attention test. Imagine a completely known population of 100 students. Forty attended the workshop; fifty met the criterion. Does knowing a student attended change the probability that they met the criterion?</p><p>In this constructed example, we can change how many students belong to both groups without changing the total number in either group. These are synthetic data, not evidence about the effectiveness of workshops.</p><div class="clt-overview"><p><strong>Learning goals</strong></p><ol><li>Identify the numerator and denominator of a conditional probability.</li><li>Distinguish a conditional probability from its reverse, a joint probability and a marginal probability.</li><li>Determine whether two events are independent in a known probability model.</li><li>Distinguish independence from mutual exclusivity.</li></ol><p><strong>Before starting:</strong> Review fractions, percentages, categorical variables and basic probability.</p></div></div>
~~~

## Make a prediction and explore

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson cp-lesson" id="cp-lesson"><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="prediction"><legend>If we know the student attended the workshop, how many students belong in the denominator?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-prediction" value="100"> All 100 students.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-prediction" value="40"> The 40 students who attended.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-prediction" value="50"> The 50 students who met the criterion.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check prediction</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><section class="clt-simulator" aria-labelledby="cp-explore"><h2 id="cp-explore">1. Explore the relationship between two events</h2><p><strong>A:</strong> attended the workshop (40 students). <strong>B:</strong> met the attention criterion (50 students). One student is selected uniformly at random.</p><div class="clt-control"><label for="cp-overlap">Number who attended and met the criterion: <output data-output="overlap">30</output></label><input type="range" id="cp-overlap" min="0" max="40" step="1" value="30" aria-describedby="cp-overlap-help"><span id="cp-overlap-help" class="clt-help">Use the slider or arrow keys to change the overlap from 0 to 40. Both marginal totals stay fixed. Changing overlap clears the simulation.</span></div><div class="clt-action-row" role="group" aria-label="Choose example population"><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary" data-overlap="30">Starting example</button><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary" data-overlap="20">Independent</button><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary" data-overlap="0">Mutually exclusive</button></div><div class="clt-control"><label for="cp-query">Which probability are we calculating?</label><select id="cp-query"><option value="b">P(B) — met criterion</option><option value="a">P(A) — attended workshop</option><option value="both">P(A and B) — both events</option><option value="either">P(A or B) — at least one event</option><option value="bGivenA" selected>P(B | A) — met criterion given attended</option><option value="bGivenNotA">P(B | not A) — met criterion given did not attend</option><option value="aGivenB">P(A | B) — attended given met criterion</option></select><span class="clt-help">Changing the question changes which students belong in the denominator and numerator. Existing simulated draws are retained.</span></div><h3>Read the contingency table</h3><table class="cp-table"><caption>Population counts and their roles in the selected probability</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Workshop</th><th scope="col">Met criterion (B)</th><th scope="col">Did not meet (not B)</th><th scope="col">Total</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Attended (A)</th><td data-cell="0"><strong>—</strong><span class="cp-cell-role"></span></td><td data-cell="1"><strong>—</strong><span class="cp-cell-role"></span></td><td>40</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Did not attend</th><td data-cell="2"><strong>—</strong><span class="cp-cell-role"></span></td><td data-cell="3"><strong>—</strong><span class="cp-cell-role"></span></td><td>60</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Total</th><td>50</td><td>50</td><td>100</td></tr></tbody></table><div class="cp-result" role="status" aria-live="polite"><p><strong><span data-output="query">—</span>: <span data-output="fraction">—</span> = <span data-output="probability">—</span></strong></p><p>Numerator: <span data-output="numerator">—</span> · Denominator: <span data-output="denominator">—</span> · Outside denominator: <span data-output="outside">—</span></p></div><h3>See the denominator change</h3><div class="cp-grid-wrap"><div class="cp-grid" data-grid aria-hidden="true"></div><div class="cp-legend"><span><i class="cp-key num" aria-hidden="true"></i>Counted in numerator</span><span><i class="cp-key den" aria-hidden="true"></i>Other eligible students</span><span><i class="cp-key" aria-hidden="true"></i>Outside denominator</span></div><p class="clt-help" data-output="grid-summary"></p></div><p class="clt-caption">The first four rows represent the 40 workshop attendees and the last six rows the 60 non-attendees. Within each group, those meeting the criterion appear first. The numerator is always a subset of the denominator.</p><h3>Compare the conditional and marginal probabilities</h3><div class="cp-bars"><div><div class="cp-bar-label"><span>P(B) · all students</span><strong data-output="marginal">—</strong></div><div class="cp-track marginal" aria-hidden="true"><span data-bar="marginal"></span></div></div><div><div class="cp-bar-label"><span>P(B | A) · attended</span><strong data-output="attended">—</strong></div><div class="cp-track" aria-hidden="true"><span data-bar="attended"></span></div></div><div><div class="cp-bar-label"><span>P(B | not A) · did not attend</span><strong data-output="not-attended">—</strong></div><div class="cp-track" aria-hidden="true"><span data-bar="not-attended"></span></div></div></div><div class="cp-result"><p><strong data-output="independence">—</strong></p><p data-output="independence-detail"></p></div><p class="clt-caption">These are exact probabilities in a known model, not conclusions from a statistical significance test. Association does not establish causation.</p></section><section class="clt-simulator" aria-labelledby="cp-sim"><h2 id="cp-sim">2. Estimate the probability through repeated draws</h2><p>Draw a student uniformly at random from the current population, return them to the population, and repeat. Every draw is independent. The two events within a single draw may or may not be independent.</p><div class="clt-action-row" role="group" aria-label="Draw students"><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary" data-draw="1">Draw 1</button><button type="button" class="clt-btn" data-draw="100">Draw 100</button><button type="button" class="clt-btn" data-draw="1000">Draw 1,000</button><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary" data-action="reset">Reset</button></div><p class="clt-status" data-output="status" role="status" aria-live="polite">Ready. Draw a student to begin.</p><p>Most recent draw: <strong data-output="latest">No draws yet.</strong></p><table class="clt-summary"><caption>All simulated draws, for the selected probability</caption><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Total draws</th><td data-output="total">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Draws in denominator</th><td data-output="eligible">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Draws in numerator</th><td data-output="counted">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Observed probability</th><td data-output="empirical">—</td></tr></tbody></table><table class="cp-table"><caption>Observed counts in all four categories</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Workshop</th><th scope="col">Met criterion</th><th scope="col">Did not meet</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Attended</th><td data-output="observed-0">0</td><td data-output="observed-1">0</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Did not attend</th><td data-output="observed-2">0</td><td data-output="observed-3">0</td></tr></tbody></table><p class="clt-caption">The observed fraction estimates the selected theoretical probability. If no draws satisfy the conditioning event, the conditional probability cannot yet be estimated. More draws generally improve precision but do not guarantee exact agreement. Each run is limited to 20,000 draws.</p></section></div>

## Interpret what you find

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson cp-lesson"><ol><li>Start with overlap = 30. Compare P(B), P(B | A), P(A | B), and P(A and B). Write each as a fraction and explain why their denominators differ.</li><li>Select P(B | A) and draw 1,000 students. Compare the observed probability with 75%. Change the question to P(A | B) without drawing new students. What changes in the observed fraction?</li><li>Choose the Independent scenario. Compare all three bars. Explain why P(B | A) equals P(B) even though some students belong to both groups.</li><li>Choose Mutually exclusive. Explain why the intersection is zero but the events are not independent. Then change overlap to 40 and compare the conditional probabilities.</li></ol><p><strong>Think about it:</strong> If workshop attendees are more likely to meet the criterion, can we conclude the workshop caused the difference? What other factors could influence attendance and performance?</p></div>
~~~

## What is conditional probability telling us?

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson cp-lesson"><p>A <strong>marginal probability</strong> describes one event among all possible outcomes, such as P(B) = 50/100. A <strong>joint probability</strong> describes two events occurring together, such as P(A and B). A conditional probability restricts the set of possible outcomes to those satisfying the condition. In the starting population, P(B | A) = 30/40 = 0.75, but P(A | B) = 30/50 = 0.60. The overlap is unchanged; the denominator changes.</p><div class="cp-formula"><strong>Probability rules</strong><br>P(B | A) = P(A and B) / P(A), provided P(A) &gt; 0<br>P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A)<br>P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)<br>Independence: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)</div><p><strong>Why this makes sense:</strong> Conditioning changes the reference group. If knowing A occurred does not change the probability of B, then A and B are independent. Here P(A) = .40 and P(B) = .50, so independence requires a joint probability of .20, or 20 students. In that case the proportion meeting the criterion is 50% both among attendees and among non-attendees.</p><p>Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together. At overlap = 0, P(A and B) = 0, but P(A) × P(B) = .20. These events are dependent: knowing that A occurred rules out B. Events with positive probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent. The word “or” in probability is inclusive: count students belonging to either group or both, without counting anyone twice.</p><p>In real research, a finite observed sample rarely matches independence exactly even when variables are independent in the population. Week 13 will introduce inference about categorical association using chi-square tests. Neither conditional probability nor a statistical association establishes a causal effect.</p></div>
~~~

At overlap = 30, what is P(B | A)?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-conditional" value="30"> 30%</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-conditional" value="60"> 60%</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-conditional" value="75"> 75%</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="direction"><legend>2. At overlap = 30, what is the denominator of P(A | B)?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-direction" value="40"> 40 attendees</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-direction" value="50"> 50 students meeting the criterion</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-direction" value="100"> All 100 students</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="independence"><legend>3. With the two fixed margins, how many students must be in both groups for independence?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-independence" value="0"> 0</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-independence" value="20"> 20</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-independence" value="40"> 40</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="exclusive"><legend>4. If no student belongs to both groups, are these two events independent?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-exclusive" value="yes"> Yes, because they never occur together.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-exclusive" value="no"> No, because both events have positive probability and their intersection is zero.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="cp-q-exclusive" value="unknown"> It is impossible to tell from the model.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><p><strong>Takeaway:</strong> Always identify the reference group before calculating a probability. Independence means the condition does not change the probability, not that events cannot occur together.</p><p>Textbook connection: OpenStax <em>Introductory Statistics 2e</em>, Chapter 3 (Probability Topics), especially independent and mutually exclusive events, probability rules, and contingency tables.</p></div>
